# R5 — Early Travel Narrative §5.1–5.4 (Luke 9:51–13:9)

**Range read in full:** raw lines 7507–8340 (slice complete)  
**Source:** Joel B. Green, *The Gospel of Luke* (NICNT, 1997)  
**Scope:** Onset of the Jerusalem journey through vigilance/repentance discourse — departure (9:51–62); 70/72; Good Samaritan; Mary/Martha; Lord’s Prayer; Beelzebul & signs; Pharisee table woes; persecution/possessions/household fidelity; fire/division; fig tree (to 13:9).  
**Voice rule:** Claims are Green’s (or Green’s reading of Luke); secondary literature only when Green cites it as support.

## Claims

### C1 — Travel Narrative: five narrative needs, not a new soteriology
**Locus:** 7507–7516 (slice ll. 1–10)  
**Quote:** "With 9:51, Luke begins a fresh section of the Gospel, sometimes referred to as the Travel Narrative.… Luke’s concerns lie elsewhere, as he foregrounds five interrelated narrative needs in his recounting of Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem."  
**Claim (Green):** After Galilee (4:14–9:50), which established messianic mission as “release” (Isa 61/58 via 4:18–19), the central section advances (1) salvation to all people / demolition of barriers; (2) division in Israel and crescendo of hostility toward Jerusalem; (3) Jesus’ necessary suffering/rejection; (4) intensive discipleship formation after disciples’ obtuseness; (5) Jesus’ “exodus” (9:31) as Deuteronomic-speech journey. Universal embrace of salvific aim is carried forward, not invented here (Mary/Simeon; poor; margins).

### C2 — Journey is literary-theological, not a travelogue itinerary
**Locus:** 7522–7526 (slice ll. 16–20, 22–26)  
**Quote:** "This way of construing the narrative of the Jerusalem journey locates the emphasis less on the idea of a travelogue, from Galilee to Jerusalem, and more on the motif of journeying and its destination, Jerusalem.… the “journey” in which Luke is interested is not about narrative structure or travel itinerary; rather, it concerns the fulfillment of God’s redemptive purpose together with the thematization of the formation of a people who will hear and obey the word of God."  
**Claim (Green):** Travel notices are nondescript/convoluted; “the way” runs from John through the journey into Acts “the Way.” Destination Jerusalem matters as culture center where God’s aim is consummated and universal mission begins. Structure: onset clear at 9:51–56 (fourfold “to journey”); end debated—Green marks end when Jesus has entered Jerusalem (19:28–48 transitional).

### C3 — Exodus intertext as Deuteronomic hearing-and-doing, not pure typology
**Locus:** 7522 (slice ll. 16–17)  
**Quote:** "Luke has built up a series of reminiscences… of Exodus material… but he has done so in a way that mimics the Deuteronomic portrayal of the Exodus journey as a series of speeches delivered by Moses to the people of God. These speeches call for faithfulness to the covenant or, in Lukan terms, for a people whose kinship with Jesus is marked by their hearing and doing the word of God (8:21)."  
**Claim (Green):** Intertextuality parodies as well as borrows; too direct Exodus mapping is problematic, but the journey is speech-and-formation oriented (cf. §12). Discipleship = hearing and doing the word.

### C4 — Journey formation “fails” until resurrection; conversion as resocialization
**Locus:** 7520 (slice ll. 14–15)  
**Quote:** "judged on these terms the journey is not successful.… enlightenment is possibly only in light of the resurrection of the crucified one (ch. 24).… discipleship as Luke has presented it requires a reconstruction of the self within a new web of relationships, a transfer of allegiances, and the embodiment of new dispositions and sensibilities."  
**Claim (Green):** 9:45 ≈ 18:34 (meaning concealed). High point 10:1–24 does not erase end-of-journey obtuseness. Luke’s audience is expected to practice “enlightened” discipleship post-resurrection; Jesus’ formation role lasts until ascension (Acts 1:1–11).

### C5 — §5.1 frame: discipleship as hearing/doing; welcome leitmotif; boundaries of Israel pushed
**Locus:** 7529–7536 (slice ll. 29–36)  
**Quote:** "The primary emphasis on the formation of a people who embody the word of God… is not discarded but heightened.… As Jesus puts it to the legal scholar, “Go and do likewise” (10:37).… what Jesus seeks is not (only) conventional hospitality but a welcome that embraces fully the message of peace."  
**Claim (Green):** Soteriological terms cluster (kingdom, peace, names in heaven, eternal life); conditions constant—do the word. Bad/good welcome: Samaritan village vs Samaritan traveler; Martha’s welcome vs Mary’s hearing. 70/72, Tyre/Sidon, Samaritan exemplar push Israel’s boundaries; open endings invite reader response (9:57–62; 10:25–37).

### C6 — 9:51 ἀνάλημψις / “taken up”: ascension (Elijah), Spirit handoff, divine resolve
**Locus:** 7545–7554 (slice ll. 45–48)  
**Quote:** "When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.… On purely lexical grounds, this reference to Jesus’ “assumption” could be taken as an allusion to his death, but the Elijah-typology… indicates that his “ascension” is in view (cf. 2 Kgs 2:10–11; Sir 48:9; 1 Macc 2:58)."  
**Claim (Green):** Fulfillment language + “set his face” (prophetic vocation) root the journey in divine purpose. Ascension links to Elisha/Spirit succession (Acts 1–2). Jerusalem destination echoes 9:31 “exodus” (death and vindication). Face/journey redundancies establish resolve and disciple role.

### C7 — Jerusalem as culture center: announcing a new world order at the center
**Locus:** 7554 (slice l. 48)  
**Quote:** "By “culture center” we mean the sacred space that establishes the order of the world… If Jesus takes this same message to Jerusalem, announcing a new worldview that undermines the world established in and by the temple, what will happen?"  
**Claim (Green):** Galilean ministry already opposed temple-emanating order but at a distance; journey dramatizes confrontation at the center. Narratological, theological, and dramatic interests intertwine.

### C8 — Samaritan village rejection; James/John fire; Jesus as Elijah type *and* antitype
**Locus:** 7556–7566 (slice ll. 50–60)  
**Quote:** "Jesus’ refusal to act according to the script provided by the ancient presentation of Elijah signals a serendipitous extension of clemency and mercy that will be matched both by the exemplary behavior of other Samaritans… and, in Acts, by the proclamation… in Samaria."  
**Claim (Green):** Messengers parallel John (prepare/before face/misread judgment). Samaritans as near-but-foreign; route into Samaritan territory notable. Rejection “because his face was set toward Jerusalem” parallels Nazareth (4:16–30)—refusal of Jesus’ embodiment of divine purpose. James/John (transfiguration witnesses) fail to collocate power with rejection; rebuked as if diabolic. Journey need re-marked: form people who hear and obey.

### C9 — Three would-be disciples: homelessness, kingdom priority over kinship, plow/fitness
**Locus:** 7568–7580 (slice ll. 62–74)  
**Quote:** "the ministry of the kingdom (v 60) and fitness for the kingdom (v 62) presume a redefinition of kinship relations centered on hearing and doing the word of God (8:19–21; cf. 14:26).… Through their attempts to delay obedience… they expose the hollowness of their affirmation (cf. 6:46)."  
**Claim (Green):** Travel notice + discipleship paired; itinerary details missing—what matters is being “on the road.” Son of Man homelessness = rejection + possessions/cares theme. Elijah let Elisha bid farewell; Jesus allows no delay. “Dead bury dead” may mean spiritually dead *or* ossuary reburial custom; either way kingdom claims trump venerable piety. Open endings address narrative and extra-narrative hearers.

### C10 — Mission of the seventy-two: symbolic universality; division as theme
**Locus:** 7582–7602 (slice ll. 83–96)  
**Quote:** "the appointment of the seventy-two can be understood as prefiguring the universal mission in Acts.… The theme of this narrative unit, then, concerns the experience of the mission as the arena of conflict and eschatological engagement with diabolic forces."  
**Claim (Green):** Read with 9:51–56 and 9:1–6; power/authority presumed from first sending; cure sick ↔ exorcism. LXX Gen 10 / 3 Enoch / Aristeas: 72 = nations. Harvest urgency; lambs among wolves; travel light. Peace as shalom entity that can rest or return; “child of peace.” Kingdom near as restoration *or* judgment. Focus on instructions/division, not a mission report.

### C11 — Woes on Galilean towns; first public “repent”; rejection of messengers = rejection of God
**Locus:** 7612–7630 (slice ll. 106–124)  
**Quote:** "This is the first use of the term “repent” in the public ministry of Jesus (though cf. 3:1–14)… Repentance has to do with redirecting one’s life toward the one purpose of God.… Verse 16… equates the rejection of his messengers with the rejection of himself and, indeed, of God."  
**Claim (Green):** Sodom as inhospitality paradigm; judgment stricter because kingdom has drawn near. Chorazin/Bethsaida/Capernaum indicted analeptically—wonder without hearing-and-doing. Tyre/Sidon (Gentiles) would have repented. “Listening” = hearing and obeying; concatenation universalizes toward Acts.

### C12 — Satan’s fall: prophetic vision of future judgment; enemy clarified (not Rome)
**Locus:** 7632–7640 (slice ll. 126–134)  
**Quote:** "Luke portrays Jesus as having a prophetic vision… whose content was the future (and ultimate) downfall of Satan, presumably scheduled for the time of the judgment.… the explicit identification of Satan as the real “enemy”… Rome is not the adversary, only one of its partners… Zechariah’s hope has not been dashed but clarified and, indeed, radicalized."  
**Claim (Green):** Mild corrective: rejoice in names written in heaven, not power. Isa 14 imagery links Capernaum’s descent and Satan’s. Fall not primordial/only-in-Jesus/resurrection—satanic activity continues (Luke 22; Acts). Authority over snakes/scorpions = satanic forces. Zechariah’s “enemies” (1:71, 74) interpreted cosmically.

### C13 — 10:21–24 christological/discipleship peak: Father–Son; infants vs wise; kingdom in envoys
**Locus:** 7642–7654; 8150–8200 area (slice ll. 150–204)  
**Quote:** "With these verses, then, we reach a christological peak in the Gospel of Luke as well as a high point in the characterization of Jesus’ disciples.… the dominion of God is historically present in the redemptive activity of Jesus and… also in the activity of Jesus’ emissaries who act… “in his name.”"  
**Claim (Green):** Same hour as 70 return; Spirit-inspired thanksgiving; reversal (Mary’s Song; poor). Father/Son filial revelation precondition of disclosure. Prophets/kings vs “you”: privileged seeing/hearing demonstrated in obedience. Missing link for disciples: integrating power/glory with suffering/rejection. Blessed eyes = kingdom present in Jesus *and* envoys regardless of reception.

### C14 — Good Samaritan: hermeneutical parable for Lev 19:18; do / do mercy
**Locus:** 8204–8218 (slice ll. 205–218)  
**Quote:** "Jesus’ closing words… return to the original question of the lawyer: “What must I do to inherit eternal life?” The parable thus serves a hermeneutical function. It interprets the summation of the law… for Luke, hearing is authenticated in doing."  
**Claim (Green):** Structure parallel two parts (motive–question–answer–imperative). Compassion language replicates God’s covenant faithfulness (1:78) and Jesus (7:13). Lawyer wants to limit neighbor; Jesus nullifies the premise—neighbor love knows no boundaries. Geography (Jerusalem road; priest/Levite; Samaritan) continues boundary-extermination toward temple center.

### C15 — Samaritan vs temple personnel: performance over ascription; exaggerated mercy
**Locus:** 8278–8290 (slice ll. 279–291)  
**Quote:** "What individualizes him is his compassion, leading to action, in the face of their inaction.… The purity-holiness matrix has been capsized. And… neighborly love has been concretized in care for one who is… self-evidently a social outcast (“the poor”—cf. on 4:18–19), and in the uncalculated disposition of one’s possessions."  
**Claim (Green):** Corpse-impurity motive for priest/Levite doubtful; status-by-birth and us-them cataloguing more central. Samaritan merchant’s care is risk-laden, non-reciprocal (cf. 6:32–36), not minimal duty. Open ending: lawyer has heard; will he do?

### C16 — Mary and Martha: hospitality redefined as attending to the word
**Locus:** 8296–8316 (slice ll. 297–316)  
**Quote:** "the welcome Jesus seeks is not epitomized in distracted, worrisome domestic performance, but in attending to this guest whose very presence is a disclosure of the divine plan.… service grounded in and brandishing moral intuitions other than those formed through hearing the word is unacceptable."  
**Claim (Green):** Not primarily contemplative vs active life tradition. Juxtaposed with lawyer: Samaritan hears-and-does; Mary listens as disciple at Lord’s feet; Martha’s “doing” censured as anxiety (8:14; 12:22). Fourfold “Lord” legitimates cultural scandal of a woman as disciple. Journey hospitality co-text (welcome/rejection).

### C17 — §5.2 Fatherhood of God: Greco-Roman *paterfamilias* qualified
**Locus:** 8318–8322 (slice ll. 319–323)  
**Quote:** "Within his own discourse situation, Luke has important reasons to qualify in what sense God is “Father.”… it was not enough simply to refer to God as “Father.” The question was (and is)… In what sense is God thus to be understood? Hence, God is presented by Luke as the Father who cares for his children and acts redemptively on their behalf."  
**Claim (Green):** Links to Mary’s hearing (10:38–42) and Jesus’ fivefold Father in 10:21–22. Against unlimited Roman paternal power (Dionysius, Gaius), Luke’s Father is nurturing/redemptive. Section ends with Father giving Holy Spirit (11:13).

### C18 — Model prayer: community formation; Qaddish/Eighteen affinities; name & kingdom
**Locus:** 8324–8368 (slice ll. 325–368)  
**Quote:** "Within its Lukan co-text, the prayer Jesus teaches his disciples is integral to the socialization of the disciples in this new community who are taught to name God as Father.… God’s eschatological work to reestablish the holiness of his name… invites them to embrace practices that honor him."  
**Claim (Green):** Prayer as identity practice (like John’s disciples’ distinctive habits), not rote empty recitation. Father = adoption/relationship/household under God, not progenitor primarily (OT election/covenant). Hallowed name echoes Ezek 36 (eschatological sanctification after profanation). Kingdom come: only God establishes reign; already present in Jesus, requiring oriented lives.

### C19 — Daily bread, forgiveness/debts, testing: patronage ripped; imitation not quid pro quo
**Locus:** 8370–8378 (slice ll. 369–377)  
**Quote:** "the prayer Jesus teaches his followers embodies the urgency of giving without expectation of return—that is, of ripping the fabric of the patronage system by treating others as (fictive) kin… The “for” of v 4b does not introduce a relationship of quid pro quo between divine and human forgiveness… Jesus spins human behavior from the cloth of divine behavior."  
**Claim (Green):** “Daily” (ἐπιούσιος) likely “bread of the coming day”—today/tomorrow/manna and/or kingdom bread (polysemic). Forgiveness of sins and debts central to “release” program (4:18–19). Testing petition: tests in Luke are detrimental to faith; disciples ask to be excused amid journey opposition.

### C20 — 11:5–13: prayer shaped by God’s character, not technology of persistence
**Locus:** 8380–8406 (slice ll. 381–406)  
**Quote:** "Luke shaped this narrative unit not with an eye to the “how-to” of pray, but with a central emphasis on the worldview leading to and informing prayer.… the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!"  
**Claim (Green):** Friend-at-midnight: friendship + honor (avoid dishonor) secure aid—echoes Father relation and sanctifying the name. Ask/search/knock universalized on needs. Lesser-to-greater: human fathers give good gifts; God gives best gift, Holy Spirit (even unrequested)—narrative need fulfilled in Acts. Disciples share Jesus’ “Father” language and Spirit destiny.

### C21 — §5.3 hostility surge: crowds join opposition; urgency of decision
**Locus:** 8408–8416 (slice ll. 408–416)  
**Quote:** "here opposition to Jesus’ ministry surfaces dramatically.… Hostility provides the horizon against which is underscored the urgency of a decision regarding Jesus. Jesus’ words… “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”"  
**Claim (Green):** Two scenes: open with crowds (14–36); house with Pharisees/lawyers (37–52), yoked by v 37a. Travel notices absent; passion predictions supply horizon. Crowds become capable of embodying opposition (not only leadership).

### C22 — Beelzebul charge: clash of kingdoms; finger of God = kingdom has come
**Locus:** 8418–8458 (slice ll. 419–458)  
**Quote:** "But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out the demons, then the kingdom of God has come to you.… Jesus positions the work of exorcism within the larger matrix of the struggle between the dominion of Satan and the dominion of God."  
**Claim (Green):** Exorcism fact not disputed—source is. Beelzebul = Satan as ruler of demons. Civil-war reductio; other Jewish exorcists also from God. “Finger of God” (Exod 8:19) legitimates Jesus; sign from heaven already given in the exorcism. Stronger man: Jesus liberates the “castle” (demonized person); not yet total defeat of Satan. Whoever not with me scatters; unclean-spirit return warns against non-ongoing faithfulness.

### C23 — True blessedness: hearing and doing over maternity status (Mary included)
**Locus:** 8462–8476 (slice ll. 463–476)  
**Quote:** "Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!… Mary is a candidate for blessedness according to the criterion set forth by Jesus.… His beatitude disallows the establishment of such conventional boundaries to divine fortune."  
**Claim (Green):** Woman’s proverbial blessing echoes Elizabeth (1:42) but needs correction. Privilege by physical descent undercut (3:7–14; 8:4–21). Mary qualifies by faith/hearing (1:45; Magnificat) not only womb/breasts. Beatitude invites all to hear and observe.

### C24 — Sign of Jonah; evil generation’s unhealthy eye; light/darkness ethics
**Locus:** 8478–8508 (slice ll. 479–508)  
**Quote:** "This generation is an evil generation… because their eyes are “not healthy.”… the request for a sign itself betrays an inner disposition oriented away from the light… and toward the realm of darkness whose head is Satan."  
**Claim (Green):** Two viable Jonah-sign readings: (1) divine rescue/vindication (future exaltation in Acts); (2) repentance proclamation. Queen of South / Nineveh as outsiders who respond will judge Israel. Eye-as-lamp physiology (light goes out): healthy/evil eye = ethical disposition. Light/darkness ↔ God/Satan (cf. Acts 26:18). Sign-seeking not benign.

### C25 — Pharisee meal: purity redefined as almsgiving solidarity; woes
**Locus:** 8510–8550 (slice ll. 511–550)  
**Quote:** "What behavior would represent the sort of purity sanctioned by God?… a purity manifest in social relations—explicitly, on a behavior, almsgiving, that collapses the distance between the social elite and the needy.… Almsgiving… was an expression of genuine social solidarity."  
**Claim (Green):** Handwashing = purity-system boundary (not OT mandate). Jesus as Lord makes inner thoughts public; Pharisees “fools,” full of greed/wickedness. Tithe without justice and love of God; honor-seeking; unmarked graves (contaminating others). Door for repentance via alms still open. Jesus authorized hermeneut of the law without negating the law.

### C26 — Lawyers’ woes: burdens; tombs of prophets; key of knowledge taken away
**Locus:** 8552–8578 (slice ll. 553–578)  
**Quote:** "scribal efforts have burdened God’s people.… you have taken away the key of knowledge; you did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering."  
**Claim (Green):** Law not the culprit; elaboration is. Tomb-building = complicity in historic rejection of messengers. Wisdom of God (Jesus’ elevated access) sends prophets and apostles—includes Jesus’ destiny and followers’ (Acts). Abel to Zechariah = whole span of Scripture’s martyrs. Result: proactive stalking (11:53–54) on the road to Jerusalem.

### C27 — §5.4 frame: one continuous discourse; vigilance leitmotif; resocialization
**Locus:** 8580–8596 (slice ll. 581–596)  
**Quote:** "from 12:1 to 13:9 Luke records what is essentially one continuous discourse… leitmotif of vigilance in the face of crisis.… This reorientation of life, to which he sometimes refers as “repentance,” involves a “theological transformation”… [and] social practices—especially vis-à-vis persecution, possessions, and issues of social relations and status."  
**Claim (Green):** Audience lines (disciples/crowds) blur; Peter’s question (12:41) thematizes universality. Crowds called “hypocrites” (12:56) as Pharisees (12:1); disciples not yet secure. Eschatological vision shapes present (kingdom gift; Son of Man as table servant; urgency of fruit).

### C28 — Leaven of Pharisees = hypocrisy as godlessness, not play-acting
**Locus:** 8598–8618 (slice ll. 599–617)  
**Quote:** "the meaning of [hypocrisy] in Luke is closely aligned with its usage in the LXX; there it describes “a person whose conduct is not determined by God and is thus ‘godless.’”"  
**Claim (Green):** Yeast = contaminant that can invade disciples; secret then public. Hidden made known: inner→outer; testing of persecution; eschatological disclosure. Persecution assumed; focus is proper response.

### C29 — Fear God not killers; sparrows theodicy; public confession and Spirit witness
**Locus:** 8620–8636 (slice ll. 619–635)  
**Quote:** "God is the only one who should be feared, but the character of God is such that one need not fear him!… for Luke, blasphemy of the Holy Spirit refers to committing apostasy in the face of persecution.… the Holy Spirit will teach you at that very hour what you ought to say."  
**Claim (Green):** “Friends” share enemies/fate/knowledge of God as Father. Gehenna = eschatological horizon. Sparrows sold yet remembered—persecution not outside God’s care (not guarantee of safety). Acknowledge Son of Man before others ↔ acknowledgment before angels. Word against Son of Man forgivable (door open for Pharisees); Spirit-blasphemy = apostasy under trial. Promise stages Acts witness.

### C30 — Rich fool and greed: life vs possessions; God-absent security
**Locus:** 8638–8674 (slice ll. 639–673)  
**Quote:** "one’s life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.… So it is with those who store up treasures for themselves but are not rich toward God."  
**Claim (Green):** Inheritance interruption patches into eschatological vigilance via possessions. Greed as status-and-wealth hunger; life = salvation metaphor. Rich farmer: good agribusiness but greed-framed; soliloquy negative; storage harms peasant economy; “fool” = one who denies God (LXX). Life on loan; woe over the rich whose possessions become security apart from God.

### C31 — Do not worry: Father’s care; strive for kingdom; little flock gift
**Locus:** 8674–8698 (slice ll. 675–697)  
**Quote:** "Instead, strive for his kingdom, and these things will be given to you as well.… Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom. Sell your possessions, and give alms."  
**Claim (Green):** Anxiety rooted in wrong theology of God. Ravens (unclean/rapacious yet fed) and lilies/grass argue lesser-greater care. “Little faith” hopeful. Nations strive for subsistence; disciples seek kingdom. Kingdom already given (Jesus’ ministry) liberates disinvestiture/alms: non-patronage reciprocity—God as Supreme Benefactor; treasure in heaven; heart follows treasure. Contrasts Pharisees (11:39–41) and rich fool.

### C32 — Household vigilance: Son of Man unexpected; master serves slaves
**Locus:** 8700–8730 (slice ll. 701–729)  
**Quote:** "You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an unexpected hour.… he will fasten his belt and have them sit down to eat, and he will come and serve them."  
**Claim (Green):** Eschatological timber unifies 12:1–13:9; not abrupt topic shift from possessions. Delay allowed but emphasis on certainty + uncertain timing → present fidelity. Master-serving-slaves subverts status hierarchy (Magnificat; foreshadows 22:24–27). Passover “loins girded” + lamps: readiness of mind/heart; avoid Pharisaic lack of vigilance. Thief image = unpredictability, not allegory of Jesus-as-thief.

### C33 — Steward parable: knowing-and-doing; proportional accountability
**Locus:** 8738–8758 (slice ll. 739–757)  
**Quote:** "From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required.… Who then is the faithful and prudent manager…? … if that slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed…’ and if he begins to beat the other slaves… and to eat and drink and get drunk…"  
**Claim (Green):** Peter’s “us or everyone?” → universal relevance + heightened disciple responsibility (10:21–24 knowledge). Steward provides food for household = embody master’s beneficence (cf. 10:25–37). Three outcomes: fidelity rewarded; knowing infidelity cut off with unfaithful (Judas/Israel typology possible); ignorance lighter beating. “Given” = knowledge of will, stewardship charge, and kingdom (v 32). Violence/excess echo Pharisee greed and rich fool.

### C34 — Fire, baptism, household division: judgment integral to mission
**Locus:** 8760–8796 (slice ll. 761–795)  
**Quote:** "I came to bring fire to the earth… Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but rather division!… Judgment… is integral to it."  
**Claim (Green):** Present judgment overlays future (fire/heat; baptism/cloudburst inverse parallel). Mic 7:6 family splits = consequence and confirmation of divine charge. “I came…” mission formula; baptism as consuming commission toward completion. Peace and division harmonized: peace-to-sinners generates opposition; Simeon/John foresaw division. Apologetic for community whose gospel dissolves conventional kinship.

### C35 — Crowds as hypocrites: can read weather, not the present time
**Locus:** 8796–8806 (slice ll. 797–805)  
**Quote:** "You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?"  
**Claim (Green):** Sign already present—family division as manifestation of mission and portent of judgment. Hypocrite = godless misdirection, not mere role-play; crowds joined Pharisees’ failure. Disciples still warned against same contagion. Settle with accuser “on the way”: if they judged rightly they would repent now to avoid eschatological prison (last penny).

### C36 — Galileans/Siloam and fig tree: no special sin; temporary clemency; repent now
**Locus:** 8808–8832 (slice ll. 809–831)  
**Quote:** "unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.… the unrepentant have escaped judgment not because of their relative sanctity but because of God’s mercy.… Now is the time to repent and to live fruitful lives."  
**Claim (Green):** Climax of 12:1–13:9. Rejects iniquity→disaster calculus for victims; fourfold “all.” Galileans/Pilate/Jerusalem undercurrent: Jesus Galilean pilgrim to ominous city—his death must not be misread as deserved judgment. Fig tree (contrast Ahiqar’s lack of clemency): extra year of manure/hope; sterility still threatens. Fruit-bearing = authentic hearing (John 3:7–9; 6:43–45; 8:4–15). Urgency: stay of judgment temporary.

### C37 — Jubilee/release thread continues in early journey (possessions, poor, alms)
**Locus:** 7507–7510; 8372; 8540–8542; 8692–8698 (slice ll. 5–7, 371, 541–543, 693–697)  
**Quote:** "Jesus’ mission is encapsulated so memorably as seeking and saving the lost (19:10).… Because of the centrality of “release” in Jesus’ missionary program (see above on 4:18–19)… disposition of one’s possessions signifies the dispositions of one’s heart, with both character and behavior expected to reflect the message of Jesus for “the poor.”"  
**Claim (Green):** Early travel material carries 4:18–19 release program: forgiveness of sins/debts in the prayer; almsgiving as purity and kingdom practice; care for the half-dead “poor” in Samaritan parable; sell-and-give vs rich-fool storage. Not a separate jubilee treatise in this range—Green keeps tying ethics of wealth and welcome back to inauguration speech.

### C38 — Green’s method in this range: narrative co-text, social scripts, discourse unity
**Locus:** passim (esp. 7507–7526; 8388–8398; 8580–8590)  
**Quote:** "A narratological reading of this segment… brings to the foreground the important reminder that in v 35 Jesus has not simply moved on from one topic to another."  
**Claim (Green / Green as interpreter):** Prefer Lukan narrative logic over form/redaction atomism: journey as construction; audience blurring; Roman household/friendship/hospitality scripts; Greco-Roman eye physiology; patronage critique. Secondary sources (Josephus on Samaritans; friendship literature; Ahiqar parallel) support socio-historical reading but claims about Luke’s intent remain Green’s synthesis.
